articles.title: Engineers dredged 500,000 cubic yards of sand from the Mississippi River and used it to build seven islands; six years later, the $25 million McGregor Lake project has restored 270 acres of aquatic habitat and protected 22 acres of wetlands
articles.summary: For years, sand dredged from the Mississippi River was removed to keep one of America's most important waterways navigable.
articles.body: For years, sand dredged from the Mississippi River was removed to keep one of America's most important waterways navigable. At one restoration site, engineers found another use for that material, building islands. The US Army Corps of Engineers has completed a $25 million habitat restoration project at McGregor Lake in Wisconsin, where about 500,000 cubic yards of clean sand dredged from the Mississippi River were used to construct seven islands.The project, which began in 2020, has now improved more than 270 acres of aquatic habitat while also restoring floodplain forest and protecting wetlands.McGregor Lake is a 200-acre backwater lake located in Pool 10 of the Mississippi River near Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin. It lies within the Upper Mississippi River National Wildlife and Fish Refuge, an area that supports a wide range of aquatic and terrestrial wildlife. The completed project was marked by the US Army Corps of Engineers' St Paul District on September 22, following six years of restoration work.Sand dredged from the river becomes new habitatThe project brought together two needs that might otherwise have been treated separately: maintaining the Mississippi River's navigation channel and restoring habitat in one of its backwater lakes. Dredging is routinely carried out in the river to maintain navigation. At McGregor Lake, engineers reused approximately 500,000 cubic yards of clean river sand generated through that process to create seven islands.The islands were not simply piles of dredged material. They were designed as part of a larger habitat restoration effort, with material from additional dredging placed on top to provide suitable ground for vegetation.Engineers also dredged 35 acres of backwater fisheries habitat. The deeper areas created through this work provide overwintering habitat for fish, while the dredged material was reused on the islands.The result was a project in which material removed to maintain the river's navigation channel was redirected into a new landscape intended to support wildlife.Seven islands, rock structures and shoreline workThe seven newly constructed islands are one of several components of the restoration. The Corps also built five rock features and stabilised more than one mile of shoreline. These measures were designed to reduce erosion and protect aquatic and terrestrial habitat around the lake.According to the Corps, the overall project improved more than 270 acres of aquatic habitat, enhanced more than 45 acres of floodplain forest and protected 22 acres of wetlands. The work was particularly focused on improving conditions for backwater fish species and encouraging the growth of both emergent and submerged aquatic vegetation.McGregor Lake's location within the Mississippi River floodplain makes these habitats important beyond the lake itself. The surrounding river corridor supports migrating songbirds as well as nesting bald eagles, herons, kingfishers and other bird species.Why McGregor Lake needed interventionBackwater areas such as McGregor Lake are important components of the Upper Mississippi River ecosystem. They provide comparatively sheltered environments where fish can feed, reproduce and survive seasonal conditions. Over time, however, erosion and changes in the lake's habitat can reduce the quality and variety of these environments.The restoration project was designed to address several of those problems at once. Increasing aquatic vegetation provides additional cover and habitat for fish and other wildlife, while the new islands and floodplain forest areas create additional terrestrial habitat. Shoreline stabilisation is also intended to limit erosion that can otherwise degrade habitat and alter the shape and depth of backwater areas.The Corps said the project was designed to increase the age and species diversity of self-sustaining floodplain forests while protecting aquatic and terrestrial habitat by reducing erosion.A six-year restoration projectConstruction began in 2020 and continued through 2026, with the project now reaching completion after six years. The work was carried out as part of the Upper Mississippi River Restoration programme, a federal initiative focused on improving habitat and monitoring resources along the river.The programme has been operating for four decades and has completed more than 62 habitat projects benefiting approximately 120,000 acres between Minneapolis and St Louis, according to the Corps.McGregor Lake is therefore part of a much larger effort to balance the Mississippi River's role as a major transportation route with the ecological needs of its surrounding wetlands, backwaters and forests.

articles.title: Scientists warmed a Colorado grassland for 29 years, but shrubs increased 150% while grasses and wildflowers fell 28%
articles.summary: A 29-year climate-warming experiment in Colorado has documented a major shift in a subalpine grassland, with shrubs increasing by 150% while grasses and
articles.body: A 29-year climate-warming experiment in Colorado has documented a major shift in a subalpine grassland, with shrubs increasing by 150% while grasses and forbs, including wildflowers, declined by about 28%. The findings come from one of the world's longest-running climate-warming experiments, conducted at the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory near Gothic, Colorado. In a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences titled Experimental warming decouples plant–fungal symbiont interactions and leads to a more conservative ecosystem, researchers found that long-term experimental warming shifted the vegetation from a forb- and graminoid-dominated community towards one dominated by Artemisia shrubs. The changes above ground were accompanied by changes in the soil fungal community, including declines in root-associated fungi and an increase in saprotrophic fungi. The researchers concluded that prolonged warming had shifted the meadow towards a more conservative ecosystem, with weaker associations between plants and some of their fungal partners.Warming changed the meadow's plant communityThe experiment involved warming plots at the site for 29 years. The researchers found that the long-term treatment produced a transition from herbaceous vegetation towards woody-dominated vegetation. Shrubs increased by 150% in warmed plots compared with ambient plots, while the abundance of both forbs and graminoids declined by about 28%.The change was accompanied by a shift in plant functional traits of about 20% towards more conservative values. In ecological terms, conservative strategies are associated with retaining resources for longer, rather than investing as heavily in rapid growth and resource acquisition. The researchers therefore characterised the warmed ecosystem as becoming more conservative in its use of nutrients and other resources. The experiment also produced a change in plant biomass. Aboveground plant biomass was 64% higher in warmed plots after 29 years, while belowground plant biomass did not show a significant response. This indicates that the warming treatment changed the balance of plant biomass above and below the soil surface, alongside the broader change in plant composition.Changes were also found below groundThe shift in vegetation was accompanied by changes in soil conditions and microbial communities. The researchers found that plant-available phosphorus increased under warming, while bulk soil enzyme activity declined by 10%. They suggest that the reduction in enzyme activity may be related to the greater contribution of shrub-derived, more resistant organic material to the soil.Soil organic matter, however, did not change after 29 years of warming. The researchers noted that some changes in soil carbon pools observed earlier in the experiment had not persisted over the longer period. These findings contributed to the researchers' description of the warmed ecosystem as having a more conservative nutrient and carbon economy. The study does not establish that the changes in soil communities were caused specifically by the shift in vegetation. Because the researchers sampled the ecosystem at a single point after the long-term treatment, they could not determine whether changes in plants caused changes in fungi, whether fungal changes contributed to the plant shift, or whether both were responses to warming.Plant-fungal relationships became weakerThe researchers also found changes in the fungi associated with plant roots. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi form relationships with plants in which the fungi can help their hosts obtain nutrients from soil while receiving carbon from the plants. The study found that root-associated fungal colonisation declined under warming. The paper's abstract reports that arbuscular mycorrhizal fungal and septate root colonisation both declined by about 17% to 20% under the warming treatment.The relationship between plants and AM fungi also became less tightly coupled. Under ambient conditions, plant and AM fungal communities were strongly associated with one another, but this relationship weakened under warming. At the same time, saprotrophic fungi, which obtain nutrients by breaking down organic material rather than forming mycorrhizal partnerships with living plants, increased by about 10%. The researchers interpret these changes as evidence that the ecosystem's dependence on plant-fungal nutrient partnerships was changing alongside the shift in vegetation. They suggest that weaker plant-mycorrhizal associations could affect nutrient transfer and contribute to the more conservative nutrient and carbon economy observed in the warmed plots.The 29-year experiment captured changes that short studies can missThe length of the experiment is significant because many experimental warming studies operate for much shorter periods. A nearly three-decade treatment allowed researchers to examine ecological responses that developed over a much longer period. After 29 years, the warmed plots differed from the ambient plots in plant composition, plant functional traits, biomass allocation and relationships between plants and soil fungi. The authors describe the resulting community as having shifted from a forb- and graminoid-dominated grassland towards a shrub-dominated and more conservative state. The researchers also note that the findings should not automatically be assumed to apply in exactly the same way to every mountain ecosystem. The response of vegetation and soil organisms to warming can vary depending on local climate, soils, species composition and other environmental conditions.A separate experiment is examining earlier snowmeltThe researchers are also investigating another consequence of changing mountain climate: the timing of snowmelt. This work is separate from the 29-year warming experiment. In April 2023, researchers began an early-snowmelt experiment at the site using 5 large plots. Snowmelt was advanced by about 2 weeks. Early results showed that mycorrhizal fungal growth advanced by about 1 week, while plant-root growth did not show a corresponding shift.The researchers are examining what this difference in timing could mean for interactions between plants and fungi. The experiment provides a separate test of how changes in the timing of seasonal conditions can affect belowground biological activity, alongside the much longer experiment examining the effects of sustained warming. Together, the studies show that long-term climate experiments can reveal changes in mountain ecosystems that are difficult to capture in shorter studies, from shifts in plant communities to changes in the relationships between vegetation and the organisms living in the soil.

articles.title: Lawsuits cost every American household thousands of dollars. Supreme Court can help
articles.summary: Supreme Court's October docket tackles climate lawsuits, digital privacy and retirement plan claims as U.S. tort costs approach $1 trillion by 2030.
articles.body: When the Supreme Court returns in October, several cases on its docket will offer a timely look at a growing problem in America’s legal system: the mounting cost of lawsuit abuse. The cases involve different industries and legal questions, but each reflects a broader fight over how far liability can extend and who ultimately bears the cost. Suncor Energy v. Boulder County, for example, could determine whether federal law precludes local climate lawsuits seeking relief for harms tied to interstate and international greenhouse-gas emissions, opening or closing a path to potentially sweeping liability for energy producers. Other cases involving digital privacy and retirement-plan claims may affect the reach of statutory liability and large-scale business exposure. SUPREME COURT CAN RESTORE SANITY AND STOP THE LEFT’S RADICAL CLIMATE AGENDA Those questions matter well beyond the parties before the court. When liability expands, businesses must account for greater legal exposure through higher insurance premiums and compliance costs as well as reduced investment. Those expenses can ultimately become a "tort tax" that increases consumer prices and the cost of goods and services purchased by taxpayers. Recent evidence suggests that the burden is growing. A new Marathon Strategies report found nearly 200 "nuclear verdicts" of $10 million or more against corporate defendants in 2025, totaling more than $25.6 billion — a 40.7% increase from the year before. More broadly, U.S. tort costs reached $529 billion in 2022, or about 2.1% of GDP, and are projected to approach $1 trillion by 2030 if recent trends continue. Economic analyses go as high as $6,000 to the average household’s annual expenses. That makes lawsuit abuse an affordability issue as well as a legal one. And the cases already before the Supreme Court tell only part of the story. While they show where some of today’s biggest liability fights have ended up, cases moving through lower courts offer a preview of the new theories that trial lawyers are testing next and that the justices may eventually be asked to adjudicate themselves. Antitrust litigation against fire-truck manufacturers offers one example. Cities, counties and fire departments allege that major manufacturers conspired to restrict competition, driving up prices and stretching delivery times. Those are serious allegations, and proven collusion should carry consequences. But manufacturers point instead to pandemic-driven demand and disrupted supply chains as explanations for the price increases and delays. Fire trucks are also highly specialized vehicles requiring custom engineering, skilled labor and rigorous safety standards. Courts should demand strong evidence before allowing those market realities to be converted into sweeping antitrust liability, and localities should think twice before supporting such lawsuits. Even unsuccessful litigation imposes defense and insurance costs that the very municipalities suing for damages may ultimately have to absorb in future purchases — meaning a lawsuit intended to recover higher fire-truck costs could end up making the next truck more expensive. A similar dynamic is emerging in the grocery aisle. Lawsuits targeting ultra-processed foods are multiplying despite early setbacks, generally alleging that major food companies marketed addictive or unhealthy products without adequately warning consumers about associated health risks. Manufacturers of specialized formula for premature infants, meanwhile, face nearly 1,700 claims alleging their products cause a serious intestinal disease. JONATHAN TURLEY: SOCIAL MEDIA ADDICTION WILL EASILY OUTLAST META'S MASSIVE MULTIBILLION-DOLLAR SETTLEMENT Both areas involve genuine health concerns, but both also show how mass litigation can gain momentum while causation remains contested. An early ultra-processed-food case was dismissed after a federal judge found correlation was not enough to establish causation, yet plaintiffs’ lawyers say they plan to appeal, continue filing similar cases and seek consolidation into multidistrict litigation. Recent evidence suggests that the burden is growing. A new Marathon Strategies report found nearly 200 "nuclear verdicts" of $10 million or more against corporate defendants in 2025, totaling more than $25.6 billion — a 40.7% increase from the year before. The formula litigation raises similar stakes. Juries have reached conflicting conclusions as the litigation has continued to expand, showing that fundamental questions about causation can remain unsettled even after a litigation campaign has grown to encompass hundreds or thousands of cases. FLORIDA SUES NETFLIX, ALLEGES STREAMER TRACKED CHILDREN AFTER PROMISING FAMILIES PRIVACY That is why these emerging legal fights deserve attention. Early setbacks do not necessarily end a new mass-tort theory. Claims can be revised and tested across jurisdictions until one gains enough traction to open broad discovery, encourage copycat filings and create pressure for industry-wide settlements. Legitimately injured consumers deserve recourse, but causation cannot become an afterthought simply because the potential pool of plaintiffs is large. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Taken together, the Supreme Court docket and these lower-court fights show the tort system at two different stages. The justices will confront liability questions that have already worked their way to the high court, while lower courts are testing theories that could become tomorrow’s major mass-tort battles. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That should strengthen the case for reform before those costs become more deeply embedded in the economy. Greater transparency around litigation funding and government contingency-fee arrangements, along with stronger screening of weak causation theories, can preserve legitimate claims while making abuse harder to sustain. Tort reform is not about protecting wrongdoers. It is about preventing an aggressive lawsuit economy from becoming another hidden cost American families are forced to absorb. articles.title: A solar-powered pump installed at California's Santa Susana Field Laboratory in 2024 has removed more than 65,000 gallons of contaminated groundwater in two years, nearly 70% of everything pumped there since 2017
articles.summary: A small shift in how groundwater is collected is making a measurable difference at California's Santa Susana Field Laboratory.
articles.body: A small shift in how groundwater is collected is making a measurable difference at California's Santa Susana Field Laboratory. According to a report by the U.S. Department of Energy, the solar-powered pumping system installed in 2024 has already removed more than 65,000 gallons of contaminated groundwater from one cleanup area, accounting for nearly 70% of all the water pumped from the site since cleanup efforts began in 2017. The system has allowed the U.S. Department of Energy to move from a labor-intensive pumping process to a more frequent, automated operation, increasing the amount of impacted groundwater that can be captured and sent for treatment.A faster approach to groundwater removalAccording to the online report, the pump operates at the Former Sodium Disposal Facility, or FSDF, in Area IV of the Santa Susana Field Laboratory and the Department of Energy is responsible for remediation of the area, where liquid metals and nuclear energy research was previously conducted at the Energy Technology Engineering Center. Before the automated system was installed, groundwater removal relied on manually lowering a pump into a well through a borehole. The process limited how frequently water could be collected and required personnel and equipment to operate the system.That changed in May 2024, when DOE completed installation of a solar-powered automated pumping system. It became fully operational the following month, adds the report.The new setup can pump groundwater seven days a week, without relying on electricity from the grid or a generator. That has allowed the cleanup operation to run more consistently while increasing the volume of water that can be removed from the affected area.65,000 gallons removed in two yearsAs of August, the solar-powered system had removed more than 65,000 gallons of contaminated groundwater. That represents almost 70% of the roughly 94,000 gallons removed from the FSDF since DOE began manually pumping groundwater in 2017. The figures highlight how significantly the newer system has accelerated removal at the site. Water captured through the cleanup effort is not released back into the environment. Instead, it is transported to a certified off-site facility, where it undergoes treatment and safe disposal.The pumping is part of interim cleanup measures designed to capture and remove contaminated groundwater and help protect surrounding groundwater resources while broader remediation work continues.Turning sunlight into a cleanup toolAccording to the department, the system also demonstrates how relatively simple infrastructure can support long-running environmental work. By using solar power to operate automated equipment, the FSDF pump can continue collecting groundwater without the logistical demands associated with conventional power sources.For a cleanup site where groundwater removal has been underway for nearly a decade, the change has produced a notable result in just two years. More than 65,000 gallons have now been taken out of the ground, treated and safely disposed of, adding another chapter to the ongoing effort to address contamination at the former research facility.Images Courtesy: U.S. Department of Energy

articles.title: A brightly striped wasp spider has been recorded in Cheshire for the first time; Chester Zoo says the harmless species is moving north as warming reshapes where British wildlife can survive
articles.summary: A striking yellow-and-black spider has turned up in Cheshire for the first time, giving conservationists another glimpse of how Britain’s wildlife is
articles.body: A striking yellow-and-black spider has turned up in Cheshire for the first time, giving conservationists another glimpse of how Britain’s wildlife is responding to a changing climate. The discovery was made during a biodiversity survey on the Chester Zoo estate, with the finding confirmed by an expert from the British Arachnological Society. According to Chester Zoo, the primary source for the discovery, the spider, nicknamed “Wendy”, is part of a species whose range has been moving northwards as warmer conditions become more common.A first record for CheshireThe spider is a wasp spider, Argiope bruennichi, an orb-weaving species recognised for the bold yellow, white and black pattern across the female’s abdomen. Its appearance can make it look more like a wasp than a spider, but the resemblance is only visual. The species is harmless to people and is not considered a threat to humans. Wendy was spotted by Rosie Cooper, an estate biodiversity assistant at Chester Zoo, while she was carrying out fieldwork. The discovery happened during a wider survey of plants and wildlife on the zoo’s estate.Chester Zoo conservationists made the discovery while working with RECORD, Cheshire’s local environmental records centre. The identification was then confirmed by a British Arachnological Society expert, establishing the sighting as the first recorded wasp spider in Cheshire. The spider itself is relatively large compared with many species commonly seen in Britain. Chester Zoo said wasp spiders can measure around 2-3cm across the body and build ornate webs among vegetation. Their webs can also feature a conspicuous vertical band of white silk, a characteristic associated with the species.Why the spider is moving northAlthough the wasp spider is new to Cheshire records, it is not new to Britain. The species was first recorded in the UK in 1922 at Rye in East Sussex and has since become widespread in southern England. According to the British Arachnological Society, it is now spreading northwards. The species needs a prolonged period of warm weather to reproduce successfully, along with relatively mild winters. As Britain’s climate changes, conditions suitable for the spider are becoming more common in areas farther north than its traditional range. That makes the Cheshire sighting more than an unusual wildlife encounter. It is also an example of how changing environmental conditions can influence where species are able to live.Ruby Merriman, Chester Zoo’s estate biodiversity manager, said the species is slowly moving north because parts of its southern European range are warming too quickly for the spiders to remain there in the same way. Chester Zoo described animals shifting their ranges in response to climate change as “climate refugees”. The movement does not mean that every individual spider has suddenly travelled hundreds of miles north. Instead, species can gradually expand their range over generations as suitable habitat and climate conditions appear in new places.What makes the wasp spider distinctiveThe female wasp spider is particularly easy to recognise. Its abdomen carries the vivid yellow, black and white markings that give the species its common name, while its legs are also striped. Males are considerably smaller and have much less striking colouring. The spider hunts from the centre of its orb web, where it waits for insects to become trapped. Grasshoppers and crickets are among its preferred prey, although flies and other insects can also form part of its diet.Its life cycle is also closely connected to the seasons. Adults mature around August and September. After mating, the female produces an egg sac that is attached to vegetation, with the young remaining protected inside until the following spring. Adult females die during autumn. Despite its dramatic appearance, there is little reason for people to be concerned if they encounter one. Chester Zoo specifically describes the species as completely harmless to humans.A small spider with a bigger climate messageThe discovery comes from an unusually diverse area of habitat. Chester Zoo’s estate covers about 205 hectares, including wet meadows, ponds, reedbeds, grasslands, woodlands, orchards and hedgerows. The area supports species including harvest mice, great crested newts and badgers, while barn owls also nest there. For conservationists, the arrival of the wasp spider therefore fits into a much wider picture. Some wildlife species are expanding into areas where conditions have become more suitable, while others face increasing pressure as their established habitats become warmer, drier or otherwise less suitable.Scott Wilson, Chester Zoo’s head of field programmes, said the arrival of Wendy was exciting but also part of a broader trend linked to climate change. He pointed to changes being observed in ecosystems around the world and said European spiders are among the wildlife groups experiencing difficulty as climates shift. The Cheshire sighting does not, on its own, prove that climate change caused this individual spider to appear there. However, the species’ established northward expansion, combined with its dependence on warm conditions and milder winters, makes the discovery part of a broader pattern already documented by British arachnologists.For now, “Wendy” is simply an eye-catching new record for Cheshire. But her presence also offers a visible reminder that the map of British wildlife is not fixed. As temperatures and seasons change, the places where different plants and animals can survive may change with them.

articles.title: Scientists found a new amoeba in California's Lassen Volcanic National Park that can reproduce at 145°F, stay active at 147°F and recover after five minutes at 158°F, setting a new heat record for complex life
articles.summary: In the steaming pools of California’s Lassen Volcanic National Park, life has found a way to thrive where most cells would begin to fall apart.
articles.body: In the steaming pools of California’s Lassen Volcanic National Park, life has found a way to thrive where most cells would begin to fall apart. Hidden in geothermal waters, a newly identified amoeba is pushing the known limits of how much heat complex life can tolerate, challenging long-held assumptions about the survival of cells with intricate internal structures, states an online report by NASA.The organism, named Incendiamoeba cascadensis and informally known as the fire amoeba, can reproduce at temperatures reaching 145°F (63°C), states the NASA website. It remains active at 147°F (64°C), moving through the scorching water in search of food. Researchers also found that it can recover after being exposed to 158°F (70°C) for five minutes. The findings, published in Cell, establish a new upper temperature record for known eukaryotes.A record for complex cellsAccording to NASA, the discovery is particularly striking because I. cascadensis is a eukaryote, a group whose cells are far more structurally complex than those of bacteria and archaea. Eukaryotic cells contain a nucleus that protects genetic material along with membrane-bound structures such as mitochondria and the endoplasmic reticulum. Those internal components perform essential jobs but can also create vulnerabilities under extreme conditions, the report adds.Heat can cause proteins to lose their proper structure, damage DNA and destabilize cell membranes. Researchers had previously suggested that the membranes surrounding eukaryotic organelles could not remain stable above about 144°F (62°C). As per the report, before its discovery, the upper temperature limit for eukaryotic life was about 140°F (60°C), based on a handful of heat-tolerant fungi and red algae. The new organism demonstrates that at least one type of complex cell can function at significantly higher temperatures.Built for a hostile environmentTo understand how the amoeba manages such intense heat, the research team sequenced its genome and examined which genes became more active at different temperatures. The results revealed several potential survival strategies. Some genes help protect and stabilize DNA, while others are involved in sensing changes in the surrounding environment. At elevated temperatures, genes associated with maintaining the correct folding of proteins became more active.The researchers also identified proteins with unusually high positive surface charges. Similar characteristics have been observed in proteins produced by heat-loving bacteria and archaea, suggesting that some of the molecular strategies used to withstand extreme heat may cross the boundaries between very different branches of life.The amoeba stops reproducing once temperatures rise above 145°F, but it can continue moving at slightly higher temperatures. Its ability to recover after a brief exposure to 158°F adds another layer to its unusual heat tolerance.What makes an extremophile?As per NASA, organisms capable of thriving under environmental conditions that would be lethal to most life are known as extremophiles. Those adapted specifically to extreme heat are called thermophiles. For an organism to qualify as a true heat-loving thermophile, it must be able to carry out essential activities such as growing, feeding, moving and reproducing above 113°F (45°C).Much of what scientists know about life in extreme heat comes from bacteria and archaea. Their comparatively simple cellular organization is thought to make them better suited to environments where heat, acidity, radiation or other stresses can damage delicate cellular machinery. Eukaryotes were considered more vulnerable because their cells contain numerous membrane-bound components. The fire amoeba suggests that this complexity does not necessarily impose such a strict temperature ceiling.Clues for the search beyond EarthThe discovery also has implications far beyond Lassen Volcanic National Park. Astrobiologists study extremophiles to understand the physical and chemical boundaries within which life can survive. Those limits can help scientists determine which environments on other worlds might potentially support life. The researchers found another intriguing clue while comparing the amoeba’s genetic information with environmental DNA collected from geothermal sites around the world. Related sequences appeared in samples from places including New Zealand and Yellowstone National Park. That raises the possibility that I. cascadensis is not an isolated oddity. Similar heat-tolerant amoebas could be living in geothermal environments elsewhere, waiting to be identified.

articles.title: Trump dismantled U.S. climate policy. But his war is cutting emissions.
articles.summary: President Donald Trump dismisses climate change as a hoax. He calls federal policies aimed at curbing it a wasteful “Green New Scam.” His administration has...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump dismisses climate change as a hoax. He calls federal policies aimed at curbing it a wasteful "Green New Scam." His administration has worked furiously to gut such policies and unleash unbridled consumption of fossil fuels.

But the Trump agenda has inadvertently dealt a sizable blow against global warming.

His war on Iran, now in its seventh month, has led to a plunge in the consumption of oil and gas around the world as fighting disrupts production and transportation.

Analysts had initially forecast that the shortages would be just a blip in the global economy, with the conflict winding down quickly and fuel exports ramping right back up to where they were. That is not how things are playing out.

The shortages have gone on for so long that they are aggressively driving down how much carbon is being released into the atmosphere, a Washington Post analysis of data from the International Energy Agency shows. People worldwide are using significantly less oil and gas, which means less climate pollution.

These charts show how the revised 2026 forecasts for oil, gas and coal use from the International Energy Agency have markedly changed the emissions outlook. They build on a development first spotted by the outlet CarbonBrief.

In January, IEA forecasts anticipated big increases in emissions from the fossil fuel sector compared with 2025. By this month, the outlook had changed drastically. Even with a spike in coal burning, as countries race to replace the oil and gas they can no longer access or afford, fossil fuel emissions this year are on track to be significantly lower than they were last year.

Such an annual decline has not happened since the height of the coronavirus pandemic. Fossil fuel consumption dropped significantly more then, and consumption was lower in absolute terms, too. Crude oil demand averaged 91 million barrels per day in 2020, compared with 102 million barrels per day under the latest IEA forecast.

But this year's drop - especially given the sharp increase that was initially forecast - is substantial.

The IEA analysis suggests global demand for oil in 2026 will decline 2.5 percent compared with last year. That would erase the amount of greenhouse gas emissions created by 42 million internal combustion engine cars.

And the IEA had initially projected the world's appetite for oil and gas would grow significantly over last year, so much so that the difference between its January projections and what is actually happening is the equivalent of avoiding the emissions from 103 million cars.

The open question is how much of the drop in oil and gas use - known in the industry as "demand destruction" - is permanent. That is hotly debated in the energy industry, with many forecasts showing demand returning to prewar levels in 2027.

But economists generally agree that the longer an energy disruption persists, the more permanent the shift may be.

Drivers burdened by gas shortages and soaring prices turn to hybrids and fully electric vehicles. Utilities unable to get shipments of liquefied natural gas shift to wind, solar and nuclear power. Homeowners trade in their oil-burning furnaces for heat pumps and rooftop panels. The economics of budding technologies, such as geothermal power, start to look more attractive, leading to infrastructure investments that permanently shift what energy is consumed for decades.

Some of these shifts are already playing out around the globe.

"The IEA expects 2027 demand to barely recover to pre-conflict levels, and a portion of demand destruction may be permanent," Pavel Molchanov, an investment strategy analyst at Raymond James, assessed in an email this month.

DNV, a multinational consultancy that models global energy demand, has dropped the assumption held by many in the industry that oil and gas consumption will come roaring back.

"It is time to acknowledge that we could all be wrong," the firm wrote in a report a few weeks ago. It noted how EV sales are surging in some parts of the world, and how expected sustained high prices of diesel - regardless of when the war ends - could reshape the shipping industry. It pointed out how the shortage of natural gas in Europe at the outset of Russia's full-blown invasion of Ukraine in 2022 led to a permanent shift away from imported energy. Renewables installations have surged on the continent since then.

"For every month the conflict lasts," DNV wrote of the war in Iran, "the probability of permanent demand destruction increases."

articles.title: DNA from Thomas Jefferson's hair delivers compelling new evidence in centuries-old paternity mystery
articles.summary: New DNA evidence from Richard Kurin's book "History by a Hair" reportedly confirms Thomas Jefferson fathered children with Sally Hemings at Monticello. A historian shared insights.
articles.body: A centuries-old question over Thomas Jefferson's relationship with Sally Hemings, a woman he enslaved, is back in the spotlight — and new DNA evidence reinforces what historians have long concluded. The Thomas Jefferson Foundation, which owns and operates Monticello, addressed the new findings in a recent statement ahead of the publication of anthropologist Richard Kurin's book, "History by a Hair." The book details an effort to analyze strands of hair linked to Jefferson, including hair discovered between the pages of an unpublished manuscript associated with him. DISCOVERY AT MONTICELLO REVEALS CONSTRUCTION SECRETS THOMAS JEFFERSON LEFT OUT OF MAPS AND LETTERS Using those genetic comparisons, researchers modeled competing paternity scenarios involving Jefferson, plus his brother Randolph and Randolph's sons. The analysis found the odds that Jefferson fathered neither Madison Hemings nor Eston Hemings were less than one in 1,000. In a statement, the Thomas Jefferson Foundation said the findings reinforce, rather than rewrite, the historical record. "The study doesn't change what we know about Thomas Jefferson, Sally Hemings, their children or their world," the foundation said. "But it offers occasion to reflect on how we came to know it, and why we share that knowledge." DNA CRACKS CENTURIES-OLD MURDER MYSTERY INVOLVING ONE OF HISTORY'S MOST FAMOUS FAMILIES "Together, these histories give us a fuller picture of Monticello, of Jefferson and his world, and of the generations of Americans who have worked to realize the Declaration's promise," the foundation added. Fox News Digital reached out to the Thomas Jefferson Foundation for further comment. Leigh Fought, professor emerita of history at Le Moyne College in DeWitt, New York, and author of the book "Sally Hemings: Given Her Time," also said the new evidence reinforces what historians had already known. "This should close the case with a lock," Fought, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital. REVOLUTIONARY WAR ARTIFACTS UNEARTHED AT SITE OF INFAMOUS COLONIAL AMERICAN HEIST: 'VERY SURPRISED' "I was already positive that the case should have been closed. No other historical event, especially of that time, has had to amass this much evidence to say it happened." Rumors that Jefferson fathered children with Hemings circulated during his lifetime and persisted for generations, Fought said, while a 1998 DNA study largely settled the question for historians. The 1998 study found a genetic link between a male-line descendant of Hemings' son Eston and the Jefferson male line. Fought said skeptics continued to advance alternative theories, including that Jefferson's brother, Randolph, could have been the father of Hemings' children — an explanation she said the new evidence rules out. articles.title: Google is sending an AI satellite into space next week
articles.summary: Google is about to launch a satellite into space equipped with its AI processors. The mission is part of Google’s Project Suncatcher initiative that could eventually put AI data centers into space.
articles.body: Google is getting ready to launch a satellite with its AI processors to test how well they perform in space, as reported earlier by The New York Times. The move is part of Google’s Project Suncatcher, the company’s experimental initiative that could eventually put AI data centers into orbit. The satellite, equipped with Google’s Tensor Processing Units, will launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket on October 1st, allowing it to harness the power of the sun in low Earth orbit. As noted by Google, the goal of the mission is to measure how well its TPUs “handle the physical stress of spaceflight and the radiation and thermal extremes of space.” [Media: This is just one step toward Google’s goal of putting a constellation of chip-equipped satellites into space — an idea Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt have also floated as an alternative to data centers on Earth. Google plans to put two satellites into orbit next year. During testing, Google found that its TPUs can withstand high levels of g-force and radiation, but notes that “some things can only be tested in space.” It’s also planning to try out a cooling system that involves heat pipes and radiators while the chips are in orbit. Travis Beals, Project Suncatcher’s senior director of product management, tells the NYT that the chips can only run for about 15 minutes before they’ll need to be turned off to cool down. “Exploring space as a viable location for scalable AI compute won’t happen all at once,” Beals writes in the company’s announcement. “It takes methodical engineering, starting with proving our hardware can handle the physical and unpredictable realities of operating in orbit. This first launch is about seeing what works, identifying points of failure, and applying those findings to future missions.”

articles.title: At England's Studland Bay, replacing damaging boat anchors with eco-moorings cut scars in seagrass by 94%; researchers say the recovering meadow is also supporting a growing population of seahorses
articles.summary: At England’s Studland Bay, damage to seagrass caused by traditional boat anchors has fallen sharply after eco-moorings were introduced, with scars in one
articles.body: At England’s Studland Bay, damage to seagrass caused by traditional boat anchors has fallen sharply after eco-moorings were introduced, with scars in one trial area shrinking by 94% between 2021 and 2025. Researchers say the recovery is also creating better conditions for marine life, including seahorses.The findings come from research by Kira Dunn, carried out as part of her master’s degree at the University of Southampton, The Guardian reported. Dunn analysed monitoring data collected after the Studland Bay Marine Partnership installed eco-moorings in 2021 to reduce physical disturbance to the seabed.The study focused on areas of seagrass affected by boat moorings. In the area where 10 trial eco-moorings were installed, bare patches in the seagrass shrank by an average of 94% over five years. In another study area, traditional chain moorings remained until 2023, and the scars there reduced by 65%.Studland Bay contains one of the UK’s largest seagrass meadows. The area was designated a marine conservation zone in 2019 and provides habitat for several marine species, including the protected spiny seahorse and the occasionally recorded short-snouted seahorse.How eco-moorings protect seagrassTraditional boat moorings can disturb the seabed as chains move with the tide. This movement can create bare patches or scars in seagrass meadows.The eco-moorings used at Studland Bay are designed to avoid that movement across the seabed. Each system has a 2-metre helical screw drilled securely into the seabed. A 2-metre elasticated riser then connects the screw to a surface buoy.As the tide rises and falls, the riser stretches and retracts. This prevents the mooring equipment from repeatedly scouring the seabed and damaging the seagrass around it.The change has allowed areas that had been physically disturbed to recover. Dunn said the results showed that the seagrass was recovering after the disturbance was removed.“The results clearly show that seagrass is recovering in areas where physical disturbance has been removed. It’s incredibly encouraging to see how quickly this important habitat can regenerate when given the opportunity,” Dunn said.Seahorses and other marine life returnThe recovering seagrass is also being linked with more sightings of marine animals. Volunteer divers who monitor seahorses at Studland Bay have reported increases in their numbers since the eco-moorings were introduced.The meadow provides habitat for the protected spiny seahorse. The short-snouted seahorse has also been recorded there, although it is seen less often.Other creatures found among the seagrass include conger eels, spider crabs and corkwing wrasse. The presence of these animals shows the wider role of the meadow as an underwater habitat.Seagrass meadows are considered valuable ecosystems because they provide shelter and habitat for marine species. They also store carbon and help protect coastlines from erosion.However, seagrass meadows are declining globally. Pollution, coastal development and the climate emergency are among the pressures affecting them. At Studland Bay, the popularity of the area with leisure boaters has added pressure to the seagrass.Five years of monitoring The results are based on monitoring carried out after the Studland Bay Marine Partnership introduced the eco-moorings. The partnership includes conservation groups and boating enthusiasts, among other organisations.The comparison between the two study areas provided a way to examine how the seabed changed after physical disturbance from traditional moorings was reduced.In the first area, where 10 eco-moorings were installed in 2021, bare patches decreased by 94% by 2025. In the second area, traditional chain moorings remained until 2023, and the scars later reduced by 65%.The findings suggest that reducing physical disturbance can allow damaged seagrass areas to recover. The research also gives the partnership evidence to assess whether the same type of mooring could be useful in other areas where boats operate close to sensitive seagrass habitats.David Brown, chair of the Studland Bay Marine Partnership steering group and lead ecologist for the National Trust, said the results had gone beyond expectations. “The impact has been beyond our expectations, and thanks to robust monitoring and research, we have the science to prove how the eco-moorings benefit seagrass and all the species that rely on it,” Brown said as quoted by The Guardian.Wider use for eco-mooringsKen Collins, emeritus research fellow and diving officer at the University of Southampton and supervisor of the study, said the research provided scientific evidence for using eco-moorings to protect seagrass.“This research provides robust scientific evidence that eco-moorings are an effective tool for seagrass conservation and restoration,” Collins said.He added that the findings supported the continued use and expansion of eco-mooring schemes in Studland and other sensitive marine environments where seagrass habitats are under pressure.

articles.title: X-planes: Are they needed in the new era of drones?
articles.summary: Where do America's X-plane projects fit in an era of cheap drones?
articles.body:
There's a weird and wonderful jet flying over the US. It has the nose of anteater, parts cannibalised from other planes and a cockpit so far back the pilot depends on a camera to see where he's going.

This contraption, the X-59, might just be the future of air travel.

The X-59's owes its eccentric design to the problem of sonic booms. The shockwave created by a jet breaking the sound barrier restricted Concorde to flights over the sea and barred it from lucrative routes across the US.

Now Nasa is working around that problem using the X-59's elongated snout to flatten supersonic booms into tolerable bumps in the background.

On top of its bizarre appearance the X-59 boasts a remarkable lineage. It's the latest in a series of experimental Nasa aircraft dating back to 1947 and the first plane to break the sound barrier, the Bell X-1.

Peter Coen, a 43-year Nasa veteran who manages the programme, explains the thinking behind 80 years of X-planes. "Our approach is to pick small goals we aim to prove with flight data and we construct an airframe for that one task."

The X-plane philosophy is to "minimise goals, the more goals you have the more expensive it gets." For the X-59 it's about suppressing sonic booms on a budget and nothing else.

In the case of the X-1, flown through the sound barrier in 1947 by the legendary test pilot Chuck Yeager, Nasa knew a .50 calibre bullet travelled faster than the speed of sound. So the stumpy little aircraft was shaped like a bullet with wings added.

A mere 20 years later the X-15 rocket plane, a cylinder with tiny wings dropped from a B-52 bomber, flew to 6.7 times the speed of sound (4,520 mph) and the edge of space, paving the way for heat-resistant materials vital to the Space Shuttle.

Nasa is flying the X-59 in conjunction with community surveys to assess what people think when a supersonic boom is bent by the planes stretched nose and hushed up.

"We want to figure out what level of boom is acceptable to people on a regular basis," says Coen, who reckons his machine will sound "like a car door being closed across the street" when it flies past Mach 1, around 660mph at airline cruising altitude.

With its cockpit and ejector seat taken from a T-38 training jet, its landing gear from an F-16 fighter and engine courtesy of the F-18 this jigsaw of an aircraft was assembled by Lockheed Martin for Nasa.

A camera feeding a screen in front of the pilot relies on instantaneous computer processing to get round the lack of forward vision. It first flew in 2025 and is now breaking the sound barrier over chosen US towns.

But is there still a place for X-plane projects in a world where relatively cheap drones are being rapidly developed - not least in Ukraine's war against Russia .

Even Nasa considered an uncrewed X-59. But drones are not always a cheaper option.

Removing the pilot would have added the cost and complication of certifying a robot jet to fly fast over urban areas.

Plus the X-59 had to be big enough to resemble an airliner punching through the sound barrier, which in turn allowed space for a cockpit.

Nasa is no stranger to drone X-planes. The X-48, a scaled down model of an airliner that blends wing and fuselage to create a single lifting body, flew in 2007.

Small was beautiful for the tiny X-48 with its 20ft wingspan as this kept the programme within budget.

"It's likely that future X-planes will be uncrewed," says Coen, before adding the vital caveats "unless the technology we're researching relates to piloting or if crewing it is more cost-effective".

Guy Gratton, professor of Aircraft Test and Evaluation at Cranfield University, gets frustrated at the suggestion crewed test planes have had their day.

"There's a belief in certain quarters that drones can do everything. In Ukraine they've done amazing things with drones, but if you want to carry people you can't take short-cuts."

Gratton has tested light aircraft and stresses the importance of a human in the loop. "You lose a huge amount without pilots, you miss lessons a pilot would identify, plus it can take four times as many people on the ground to test a drone."

Staff monitoring signals from a drone are an indirect cost that keeps some piloted X-planes relatively affordable.

The UK has flown its own technology testbeds and Chris Yeo was in the pilot's seat of one. The Experimental Aircraft Programme (EAP) flew from Lancashire in 1986 and tried out core systems for the Typhoon fighter.

Yeo acknowledges the EAP's shared heritage with X-planes. "They all research some facet of flight, and demonstrate the design is working correctly. A lot of people say they can do something, but you only know it works when the design has been tested and certified."

Forty years on from Yeo's EAP flights a new UK technology demonstrator is taking shape. It is, says Tony Godbold who runs the project for BAE Systems, "the X-plane of our generation".

This BAE Systems initiative pulls together 100 UK suppliers including Rolls-Royce to test out ideas that might make it into the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP), a fighter due to fly in the 2030s. The technology demonstrator will borrow engines from the existing Typhoon and fly sometime in 2028.

This has triggered great excitement in the UK's small community of qualified fast jet test pilots. Almost every one, around 14 of them says Godbold, has already tried out this plane on a flight simulator.

For many in the aerospace industry, the human element still matters as much as it did in Yeager's day. "You can model a lot on computers and simulators, but the experience of test pilots is when stuff gets real, we only really learn things when we get their feedback," Godbold admits.

There's a political dimension to such jets too. Godbold says his plane underlines the UK's commitment to GCAP, a joint effort with Italy and Japan. "This proves we are serious in this space."

articles.title: Massachusetts is turning a retired cranberry bog into the final restored link along Red Brook; the project is designed to protect a rare brook trout that moves between freshwater and the ocean
articles.summary: Massachusetts is restoring a former cranberry bog in Plymouth and Wareham to complete protection of Red Brook from its headwaters to salt water.
articles.body: Massachusetts is restoring a former cranberry bog in Plymouth and Wareham to complete protection of Red Brook from its headwaters to salt water. The Century Bog project will turn the retired cranberry farm into a functioning wetland and stream channel, creating a more connected habitat for native species, including a rare variant of eastern brook trout known as 'salters' or 'sea run brook trout'.According to Cape, Coast & Islands, the restoration is part of the Massachusetts Division of Ecological Restoration’s Cranberry Bog Restoration Program. The programme works with farmers who want to move away from cranberry farming and put their land into conservation. The effort has become more relevant as cranberry farming has declined in Southeastern Massachusetts, with farmers retiring, climate change and falling prices linked to the growth of corporate-scale farming.Century Bog is the latest addition to the Red Brook Wildlife Management Area, which is managed by the Massachusetts Division of Fish & Wildlife. Its restoration is expected to complete the protection of Red Brook, connecting the protected area from its headwaters at White Island Pond all the way to Buttermilk Bay.The project is also aimed at helping species that depend on the connected wetland and stream habitats. Jason Zimmer, Southeast District Supervisor with the Massachusetts Division of Fish & Wildlife, said the addition of Century Bog represented the “complete protection of Red Brook from the headwaters, which are actually White Island Pond, all the way to Buttermilk Bay,” he said as quoted by Cape, Coast & Islands.Why cranberry farms are being restoredCranberry farming was once more widespread in Southeastern Massachusetts, but the industry has changed over the years. There are fewer cranberry growers in the region than there were a decade ago.The reasons include farmers retiring, climate change and falling prices as corporate-scale farming has grown. For some farmers, however, leaving cranberry production does not necessarily mean abandoning the land.The Cranberry Bog Restoration Program offers what it describes as a 'green exit strategy'. It works with state and federal programmes and environmental organisations to help farmers place their land into conservation.Zimmer said many cranberry growers have a strong connection to the land they have worked on for decades. “We certainly find that there's a pretty strong environmental ethic and kind of tie to the land in cranberry growers.”“They've worked and cared for the land for, you know, in some of these families, decades and decades. And they want to see the land continue and be protected,” Zimmer added.That approach has allowed former cranberry farms to become opportunities for wetland restoration rather than remaining in agricultural use.Century Bog to become natural wetlandCentury Bog was previously a working cranberry bog. The restoration work is focused on returning the site to a natural functioning wetland and stream channel. Heavy equipment is being used as part of the process to restore the wetland habitat.For Red Brook, the importance of the project goes beyond the former cranberry farm itself. The restored area will form part of a continuous protected stretch running from the brook’s headwaters at White Island Pond to Buttermilk Bay. Zimmer said this connection was what made Century Bog significant for the wider Red Brook area.The restoration is also expected to benefit around 60 species that Massachusetts identifies as being in greatest need of conservation. These include native fish such as herring and eel, as well as the unusual brook trout variant known as “salters”.The brook trout that enters salt waterEastern brook trout are freshwater fish, but the “salters” found in Red Brook have a distinctive behaviour. They can move into saltwater estuaries at certain times of the year.These sea run brook trout use the saltwater environment, particularly from mid-spring through the summer. Their movement between freshwater and saltwater allows them to respond to changing conditions and use food available in the estuaries.Zimmer said the fish may leave cold-water streams when the water becomes warmer. “Because of the fact that they do have access to the saltwater environment and during certain times of the year, particularly mid-spring through the summer, they'll go out into the saltwater environment,” he explained.He said the movement is partly linked to warming water in cold-water streams. The trout can also benefit from the food resources available in the saltwater estuaries of Buttermilk Bay.The restoration of Century Bog is therefore connected to the wider habitat used by these fish. Protecting Red Brook from its headwaters to the bay helps maintain that connection between freshwater and saltwater environments.Century Bog is one of several projects being carried out through the Cranberry Bog Restoration Program. So far, the programme has completed nine restoration projects. Together, those projects have restored more than 500 acres of wetlands and more than 10 miles of associated streams. Another 10 projects are currently in progress, in addition to the Century Bog restoration.

articles.title: Un agricultor de Burkina Faso recupera una técnica de cavar hoyos y llenarlos de estiércol para que las termitas excaven túneles: las tierras volvieron a ser productivas
articles.standfirst: Durante 12 años, esta región sufrió la peor época de sequía prolongada de su historia
articles.summary: Durante 12 años, esta región sufrió la peor época de sequía prolongada de su historia
articles.body: Cuando parece que todo está perdido, siempre se puede encontrar una solución gracias a la ciencia. En 1972, Burkina Faso iniciaba un periodo de 12 años de sequía prolongada, la que hasta ahora ha sido la peor etapa de su historia. La falta de agua provocó que la tierra se endureciera, generando una costra mineral llamada laterita, que impedía que en los terrenos creciese cualquier ser vivo. Sin vegetales, frutos y demás alimentos de la tierra, la población de Burkina Faso empezó a tener problemas de salud y a morir por hambruna. La mayoría de habitantes de la zona del Sahel empezaron a emigrar hacia el sur, a las ciudades más pobladas. Yacouba Sawadogo tomó la decisión contraria: volver a la aldea y probar todo tipo de experimentos para revitalizar el terreno. Para conseguirlo, llevó a cabo una práctica que había quedado en desuso con el paso de los años en esta región. Cavó sus propios hoyos y dejó que recogieran todo el agua posible en la época de lluvia. Sin embargo, introdujo una serie de variables que acabaron siendo clave para recuperar el terreno. No hizo los hoyos justo antes de los meses de lluvia, sino que los hizo durante las estaciones secas, cuando el suelo estaba más duro. Además, cada hoyo lo llenó con material orgánico, ya fuese estiércol, compost, residuos de cultivos. Por último, la zona del contorno la completó con rocas y piedras a su alrededor. Lo que consiguió fue que el material orgánico, una vez llegaron los meses de lluvia, atrajo a las termitas. Éstas fueron las responsables de ir cavando el suelo que antes estaba impenetrable. El agua penetró por toda esta tierra que llevaba muchos años completamente seca. Las raíces de los cultivos empezaron a agarrarse y el alimento volvió a crecer varias décadas después.

articles.title: Google hitches a ride aboard Elon Musk's SpaceX; sends TPUs to space; CEO Sundar Pichai says: Well, we are going to find ...
articles.summary: Google announced that its Project Suncatcher is scheduled to embark on its first test in orbit, launching a prototype satellite to evaluate how Google
articles.body: Google announced that its Project Suncatcher is scheduled to embark on its first test in orbit, launching a prototype satellite to evaluate how Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) perform in space. Sharing a post on X, Google CEO Sundar Pichai wrote: “Can our TPUs survive and operate in space? Well, we're going to find out”. He further revealed that TPUs will be sent in space onboard the upcoming Transporter-18 rideshare mission with SpaceX was developed in partnership with Planet. “Project Suncatcher is hitching a ride aboard @SpaceX's Transporter-18 mission, testing a prototype satellite built in partnership with @planet,” Pichai wrote adding “One small step for TPUs....”.SpaceX CEO Elon Musk replied to Pichai’s post with rocket emojis.What is Google’s Project SuncatcherSundar Pichai first discussed the ambitious Project Suncatcher in 2025. It is a long-term, research moonshot exploring whether space could one day host scalable machine learning infrastructure.Pichai then acknowledged that the concept “looks crazy today,” Pichai defended the moonshot initiative by arguing that it is necessary to meet the vast, exponential demands of future computing power.“I'm constantly thinking in that time frame. One example of this is Project Suncatcher two weeks ago, where we announced we're gonna build data centers in space. Obviously, it's a moonshot. Some of it looks crazy today,” he said in a Release Notes podcast this week.Pichai emphasised that Google’s strategy involves constantly thinking on a long time frame and working backward from monumental goals. For Project Suncatcher, the justification lies in forecasting the processing demands of the next generation of AI.“You know, when you truly step back and envision the amount of compute we are going to need, it starts making sense,” Pichai said, adding, “It's a matter of time, and so, how do you make progress on that? You work back, and have 27 Milestones and get underway.”Google’s first satellite for the project is set for launchOn October 1, the satellite from the San Francisco lab, which Google has named MVP, is set to take the first step toward the company’s goal. The satellite will be loaded onto a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket at Vandenberg Space Force Base near Santa Barbara, California, before being launched into orbit.You use AI every day. articles.title: The US has returned 36 ancient Syrian artifacts worth more than $5 million; 13 were seized from the Metropolitan Museum of Art, a Palmyra stone relief, 14 Roman mosaics were among the objects sent home
articles.summary: Ancient pieces of Syrian history that had traveled far from their original landscapes are now making the journey back home.
articles.body: Ancient pieces of Syrian history that had traveled far from their original landscapes are now making the journey back home. US authorities have returned 36 antiquities to Syria, a collection worth more than $5 million that includes a monumental relief from Palmyra, Roman-era mosaics and objects recovered from major private and institutional collections, states a report by Arab News. The repatriation, announced September 23, marks another major effort to trace and recover cultural objects that entered the international art market through illicit trafficking.A collection spanning centuriesAccording to Arab News, among the returned objects is a massive limestone relief from ancient Palmyra. The funerary sculpture dates to the late second century CE and depicts a reclining man surrounded by a woman and three children. Weighing more than 1,000 pounds, the relief originally formed part of a Palmyrene tomb. Investigators determined that it had been carefully removed from a burial chamber before being smuggled through Dubai.Its history is particularly significant because the relief left Palmyra before the ancient city suffered extensive destruction at the hands of ISIS between 2015 and 2017. The archaeological site, a UNESCO World Heritage site, was heavily damaged during the conflict, making the recovery of objects removed from the city especially important.The collection also includes 14 mosaics taken from a Roman villa in Syria. Among the other notable pieces is a third-century BCE mosaic section portraying the mythological wedding of Telete and Eros, created from hundreds of tiny pieces of colored stone known as tesserae.13 pieces came from the MetThe report adds that thirteen of the 36 antiquities were seized from the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York as part of investigations into the provenance of ancient objects held by the institution.The Manhattan District Attorney's Office said its Antiquities Trafficking Unit has seized 402 antiquities from the Met since 2017, with a combined value of $98.7 million. The Syrian return therefore forms part of a much broader examination of objects that passed through museums, galleries and private collections.Four other objects in the latest repatriation came from the collection of American collector Michael Steinhardt. Those pieces were among approximately 180 antiquities valued at $70 million that authorities recovered from his collection in a 2021 agreement. That agreement also resulted in a lifetime prohibition on his acquiring additional antiquities.Tracing a global antiquities tradeInvestigators linked 31 of the returned Middle Eastern and North African antiquities to objects allegedly trafficked into New York by Georges Lotfi, a Lebanese antiquities dealer who is the subject of an arrest warrant issued in 2022 and an Interpol Red Notice from 2023. The allegations against him remain subject to the legal process.The latest return adds Syria to a growing list of countries receiving cultural artifacts recovered through investigations in New York. The Manhattan District Attorney's Antiquities Trafficking Unit says it has recovered more than 6,400 cultural treasures valued at about $495 million and returned more than 6,200 of them to 40 countries.For Syria, the return represents the recovery of objects connected to civilizations that flourished thousands of years ago, and, in the case of the Palmyra relief, a tangible piece of a site whose surviving heritage has faced extraordinary losses in recent history, concludes the report.

articles.title: Colorado researchers grew the world's most expensive spice on rooftop solar panels; harvested twice the output and generated $60,000 in return while producing electricity
articles.summary: There are no limits to what a well-planned project cannot achieve and researchers in Colorado have proven it right.
articles.body: There are no limits to what a well-planned project cannot achieve and researchers in Colorado have proven it right. They have managed to make a rooftop with solar panels produce electricity while also growing the world's most expensive spice and generating extra income.Colorado State University researchers report that saffron, grown beneath solar panels rated at 40% transparency, produced twice as many flowers and twice the dried spice yield as compared to unshaded rooftop plots. The conditions on a green roof – well-drained, nutrient-poor substrates and extreme microclimates – are surprisingly ideal for saffron production. The finding points to a promising use of agrovoltaics, which pairs agriculture with solar electricity generation.A sunlit experimentThe research was conducted at the CSU Spur campus in Denver, where Jennifer Bousselot's team studies planted roofs with and without solar installations. These spaces let researchers investigate how urban rooftops could produce food where farmland remains scarce. It was in 2007 that Bousselot began studying the relationship between green roofs and solar panels.In their March 2026 research summary, Reece Bailey and Bousselot warn that “too much shade can be detrimental to saffron yield.” They propose panels that transmit 30% to 40% of the light, mounted 6 to 8 feet above the growing surface.A separate 2022 experiment in eastern Morocco compared full sun with three shade levels over 24 months and found the highest saffron yield with 30% shade. That is roughly 70% of sunlight remaining, not 30% transmission. The percentages describe different things, so the studies do not establish one universal lighting recipe for every climate and panel layout.A $60,000 figureThe Colorado team modelled five years on an existing 46-kilowatt rooftop array with 4,356 square feet of growing space. Its budget projects about $61,000 in net revenue, including electricity, dried saffron, and sales of corms (the underground structures used to grow new plants).The assumptions include $35 per gram of saffron and corms at 25 cents each. Electricity can contribute $13,470 over the five years. However, first-year costs exceed revenue and the budget does not cover building a new rooftop installation.Saffron consists of the dried red stigmas of Crocus sativus, a fall-blooming crocus harvested and processed by hand. That careful work helps explain why a tiny jar in the kitchen can carry such a large price tag.University of Vermont researchers measured just how much work sits behind the harvest. In their solar-field experiment, producing a single gram of dried saffron required 159 to 179 flowers. A larger flower count is encouraging, but it also means more flowers to pick and process before that spice reaches a customer. The timing can be useful for small farms, too. Vermont’s saffron researchers describe an October or November harvest, after much of the main growing-season rush has passed. The crop could provide additional seasonal income, although someone still has to pick the flowers and separate the delicate threads.For cities, the appeal of the project is exciting. Rooftop farming and solar generation can share the space and panel shade can reduce crop heat stress and irrigation needs under suitable conditions. CSU Extension notes that rooftop systems present installation and maintenance challenges, with planting and harvesting done by hand. In practical terms, a productive roof needs more than plants and panels. It needs a workable plan for growing, harvesting, and maintaining both systems.
